outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your text, refined for greater eloquence and flow while preserving all of the original content and imagery:

---

I was once someone's honors student—a sticker, a star. I excelled at Home Economics and Geometry; I learned to grip a fork and to steer my mother's car. Old enough to work, I replenished the salad bar at Steak & Ale, where scarcity was the one line I could never fail. During the summers between university terms, I interned at AT&T, in the minority outreach program they called Inroads. My boss, Vicki, had two roommates whom she referred to, simply, as The Gays, camped out on her floor. That was before I was gay—though I won't pretend to say so with a straight face. As if anyone truly cares; still, I care.

What I am trying to say is this: all of it prepared me for these squat, blinking office accessories—for the dry, sober regret that follows the accidental reply-all. By now, there is a great deal to lose. Little by little, I have grown so careful: no talk of politics, no mention of orientation. I let them call him "a homosexual" without offering an arched correction.

At a fondue buffet in Zurich, our dumbfounded senior group director—after I let slip, damn it, my trip with a twenty-year-old—inquired, "They're always over seventeen, right?" I assured her, of course, God yes, and, seething, smiled—the smile for which I am famous. I did not wish to frighten her. But I tell you, I am keeping score.

E-mail is nothing more than a suicide I would like, please, to recall. Note my suicide. I am paid to multitask, to wring the life out of every joy. On Monday, I will ask—each dash a loaded gun, each comma a knife—that you bury the black-box file.

---

outputs.L2:
Once, I was a high-achiever, the kind who earned gold stars and stickers. I got top marks in Home Economics and Geometry; I mastered using a fork properly and how to drive my mom's car. When I hit working age, I restocked the salad bar at Steak & Ale, and keeping the portions lean was a task I never botched. During the vacation months while I was in college, I did internships at AT&T through their minority mentorship program, Inroads. My supervisor, Vicki, shared her place with two roommates she referred to plainly as The Gays, who were sleeping on her floor. This happened back when I hadn't yet come out—I can't pretend otherwise with a straight face. Not that anybody's really invested, but I am.

Here's my point: every bit of this readied me for these little humming desk gadgets. For the bitter sobriety that follows an accidental reply-all. These days the stakes are high. Gradually, I've grown incredibly guarded—no discussing politics or sexuality. I sit quietly while someone labels a person "a homosexual," offering no pointed correction.

Over a fondue spread in Zurich, our clueless senior group director—after I carelessly mentioned, dammit, my getaway with a twenty-year-old—asked me, They're always past seventeen, aren't they? I assured her yes, absolutely, and, boiling inside, gave the smile I'm known for. I didn't want to alarm her. But believe me, I'm keeping track.

Email is nothing but a suicide I'd like to take back, please. Take note of my suicide. My job is to juggle everything, to squeeze the joy out of anything fun. On Monday I'll be asking—each dash a cocked pistol, each comma a blade—that you go and bury the black-box file.
outputs.L3:
# Reflections on a Career and a Divided Self

Looking back, my path was a conventional one. I was the student who excelled, the young professional who landed the early jobs, the ambitious candidate who secured the coveted corporate internships. Each of these milestones felt like a natural step, building steadily upon the last, shaping a trajectory that seemed both admirable and inevitable. By every external measure, I was doing exactly what I was supposed to do.

Yet alongside this outward success, something more private was taking shape. My sexual identity emerged gradually, revealing itself over time rather than arriving in a single moment of clarity. It became a source of deep personal significance—an essential part of who I am. But it also became something I learned to conceal, particularly in the workplace, where I sensed it did not belong.

To navigate my professional life, I have grown increasingly cautious. I steer conversations away from anything that might expose too much of myself—politics, personal orientation, any topic that carries risk. When colleagues make remarks I find objectionable or simply wrong, I swallow my corrections and let their words stand unchallenged. Silence, I have discovered, is often the safest strategy for survival.

This careful composure was tested recently when a senior director made an offensive assumption about my personal relationship. In that moment, I felt a surge of silent rage rising within me. But I did what I have trained myself to do: I offered a practiced smile, one that concealed the anger beneath it, and let the moment pass without incident.

Now I find myself trapped in a routine that slowly deadens the soul. The corporate rhythm continues, day after day, and I move through it with quiet resentment. I keep score of every indignity I endure, every small compromise of self, tallying them in a private ledger that no one else can see. It is a wearying existence—one of outward accommodation and inward accounting, waiting for something, though I am not always certain what.
outputs.L4:
# Keeping Score

The poem opens in the territory of memory, where the speaker excavates fragments of a life spent proving worth. There are childhood scenes—the gold stars, the report cards pinned to refrigerators, the early recognition that achievement could function as both shield and currency. These recollections arrive not in orderly sequence but in disjointed flashes, mirroring the way trauma and adaptation fracture our sense of continuity. The reader is meant to feel the discontinuity: a bright child who learned early that excellence was a form of protection, a way of earning the right to occupy space.

From this foundation, the poem moves into the speaker's entry into professional life. The early internships appear as sites of dawning awareness, where the speaker first learns the unspoken rules of corporate belonging. Here the environment is coded relentlessly heteronormative—the casual assumptions about weekend plans, the presumed girlfriends and wives, the offhand jokes that require a laugh to prove one belongs. The speaker absorbs these signals and begins the exhausting work of translation, learning which parts of the self can be shown and which must be tucked away, folded down, made invisible.

The present-day workplace forms the poem's central stage. Here the speaker moves through meetings and hallway conversations, through the performance of collegiality that the office demands. The famous gesture emerges: the smile deployed to mask discomfort, the pleasant face maintained while, underneath, the speaker is "keeping score." This scorekeeping becomes the poem's controlling metaphor—a private ledger of every microaggression, every erasure, every moment when authentic self-expression must be swallowed for the sake of survival. The smile is not warmth but armor; the tally is not vindictiveness but a form of psychological accounting, a way of remembering what the smiling costs.

At its emotional core, the poem exposes the toll of this constant self-censorship. The suppressed rage becomes almost a character in its own right, a pressure held just beneath the surface of professional composure. The speaker reveals how the daily labor of masking—of editing pronouns, deflecting personal questions, performing a sanitized version of the self—amounts to a slow erosion of dignity. What the corporate world calls professionalism, the poem suggests, is often the demand that queer workers erase their authentic identities in exchange for acceptance and advancement.

By weaving together childhood, early career, and present experience, the poem argues that this erasure is not a single event but a lifelong pattern, a continuous negotiation between visibility and safety. The fragmented structure enacts the very fracturing it describes: a self divided against itself, always calculating, always performing. In the end, the scorekeeping stands as both an act of resistance and a wound—proof that the speaker refuses to forget the price of belonging, even as they continue, smile fixed, to pay it.
outputs.L5:
# The Geometry of an Old Home

There is a particular kind of geometry that lives in old homes, one that no architect ever intended and no blueprint could predict. It emerges slowly, over decades, as houses settle into the earth and surrender to time.

Walk through an old home and you will notice how the angles have gone soft. Doorframes that once stood at perfect right angles now lean with a gentle, almost human tilt. Floorboards slope subtly toward the center of rooms, worn smooth by generations of footsteps. A marble placed at one end of the hall might roll, unhurried, toward the other. The straight lines of youth have relaxed into the curves of age.

This imperfect geometry tells a story. Each crack in the plaster follows the mathematics of stress and time, spreading like rivers across a ceiling. The staircase, its wooden steps dipped in the middle from a century of climbing, records the passage of every resident who ever hurried up to bed or descended slowly on a quiet morning. The house remembers them all in its shapes and slopes.

There is beauty in this. Modern construction chases precision—laser-measured, machine-cut, aggressively level. But an old home offers something machines cannot manufacture: the geometry of belonging. The way a room curves to embrace you, the familiar creak of a particular stair, the window that sticks just so. These are not flaws but signatures, evidence of a life fully lived within four imperfect walls.

Perhaps this is why we grow attached to old houses. Their crooked geometry mirrors our own—imperfect, weathered, and beautiful precisely because of the years that shaped them.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a confessional free-verse poem in the voice of a middle-aged gay man reflecting on his corporate career, his closeted early life, and the small indignities of office culture. Use vivid, ironic details and let bitterness simmer beneath a polished surface.
counterfactuals.output:
Exit Interview

Twenty-three years I gave them,
and what I remember is the carpet—
that industrial gray-blue meant to hide
everything, coffee, footprints, the slow erosion
of a man's particular light.

I was good at the meetings.
I could nod with the best of them,
could say *let's circle back* and *bandwidth*
and *at the end of the day*
while at the end of the day
I drove home to the condo
I told them was closer to the office,
never mentioning Daniel,
never mentioning the second toothbrush,
the way he laughed at my impressions
of the VP who called everyone *champ.*

In 1987 I learned to modulate.
To lower the register, to sit with my knees apart,
to keep the wrist a disciplined thing.
I practiced in the break room mirror
the way a spy practices a cover story,
and I was fluent, God, I was fluent—
I could pass a polygraph of small talk,
could survive the Monday inquisition,
*good weekend? do anything fun?*
Oh, the fun I did not do.
The fun I filed away.

They gave me a plaque once.
Faux walnut, a brass plate misspelling
my own name, *Excellence in Leadership,*
and I thanked them, I actually thanked them,
holding that cheap wood like a communion wafer,
tasting the whole ridiculous host of it—
the sheet cake, the applause,
the fluorescent benediction.

I was passed over twice
for men named Chad who golfed.
I did not golf. I studied the wives
at the Christmas parties,
their beautiful boredom, their good shoes,
and understood I had married the company instead,
had given it the years, the flexible spine,
the Sunday-night dread,
the body slowly forgetting
it was ever meant for pleasure.

Here is the thing nobody tells you:
the closet doesn't only close on love.
It closes on the whole self,
teaches you to shrink so early
that even after—even now, unclenched,
Daniel's ring on my finger,
the photo finally on the desk—
I flinch when someone asks
what I'm doing this weekend.

Today they took my badge.
Deactivated it while I watched,
a small green light going dark,
and I felt something almost like grief,
which is the cruelest joke of all—
that I could mourn a place
that never once
asked me my true name
and got it right.

I kept the plaque.
The misspelled one.
I'll hang it in the garage
where the light is honest
and no one's watching
how I stand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem about workplace alienation and identity that weaves together memories of adolescence, an internship, and a tense moment at a business dinner abroad. End with imagery connecting email and violence.
counterfactuals.output:
**Provisional Employee**

At fourteen I learned to fold myself
into the shape of a locker,
narrow and gray, a combination
only I could turn. I practiced smiling
in bathroom mirrors between classes,
rehearsing a face that would pass.

The internship taught me the rest:
how to answer *how are you* with *busy, good*,
how to laminate my name onto a lanyard
and wear it like a smaller, truer skin.
I photocopied someone else's certainty
for eleven weeks, unpaid, learning
the exact weight of a stapler,
the exact silence of a room
that has already decided about you.

Now the dinner in a city
whose name I mispronounce.
Seven courses, and between the fish
and the toast I do not understand,
a client leans across the tablecloth
and asks what I actually *do*—
and I feel the old locker-hinge
in my throat, the adolescent scramble
for a self to hand across the bread basket.
The candlelight makes strangers of my hands.
I laugh at the right moment. I always do.
Somewhere the boy in the mirror
is still practicing, still folding.

Later, in the hotel, the laptop opens
its blue mouth. The unread messages
stack like knives in a drawer,
each subject line a thin bright edge—
*Following up*, *Circling back*, *Per my last*—
and I answer, and answer, and answer,
pressing *send* the way a soldier
lowers a blade he was handed,
not knowing whose war it is,
only that the room expects
the wet, clean sound of yes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dramatic monologue poem where the speaker recounts their life from honor student to corporate professional, touching on being gay in a hostile office environment, using internal rhyme and dark humor.
counterfactuals.output:
**Ladder, Rung by Rung**

They pinned me with a medal at eighteen—*honor student*, clean
and gleaming, all my dreaming stapled to a transcript's sheen.
I memorized the theorems, wore my future like a suit,
too eager, too precocious, all my promise, all my loot.

My mother framed the diploma. My father shook my hand
like closing on a merger he could nearly understand.
And me? I learned to fold myself, to iron out the crease,
to tuck the truest part of me beneath a corporate fleece.

Now watch me climb the ladder, watch me flatter, watch me spin—
I traded flannel Sundays for a cubicle of sin,
where Gary from accounting calls me *buddy*, calls me *guy*,
and laughs a certain laughter that could curdle any sky.

Oh, I have *soft* hands, apparently. Oh, I *decorate* my desk.
They photograph my quirks and file them, Kafka-esque, grotesque.
I smile through every meeting like a hostage on the news—
*proof of life, I'm thriving,* while I'm surviving on the fumes.

There's dark comedy in *diversity*—they printed it in blue
on posters in the break room, where I'm welcome (*ish*) and *you*
can be *authentically yourself!* (just not, of course, out loud,
and not before promotion, and by God, don't draw a crowd).

I dated once. A stockbroker. We kissed behind a bar,
and Monday, someone saw us, and the whisper traveled far,
until my quarter *numbers*—which had always led the pack—
were suddenly *concerning*, and my *fit* was thrown off-track.

So here's my dry oration, my libation to the grind:
I am the model minority they keep but never mind.
I brought them all my brilliance, all my hunger, all my drive,
and learned that being useful isn't quite the same as *alive*.

But listen—here's the punchline, and I promise it's a good one:
the honor student's honor is the last thing I'd have won
if honor meant this hollowing, this swallowing of flame.
So I quit. I signed my resignation. Kept my burning name.

And Gary, buddy, *guy*—I hope your ceiling holds you tight.
I'm walking out the lobby into merciless, *queer* light,
where nobody's evaluating how I hold my wine,
and every crooked, honest thing I am is finally *mine*.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem titled something about corporate email or the "black-box file," narrated by an employee who feels quietly murderous rage toward homophobic coworkers while maintaining a professional smile.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Black-Box File

Subject line: *Per my last email.*
I sign it *Best,* the way I sign
a check I know the bank won't honor,
a smile bolted at the mouth's four corners.

Down the hall, they laugh at something—
a word they think is just a word,
a slur passed hand to hand like candy,
sweet in every mouth but mine.

I keep a folder no one sees.
Not on the server. Not in cloud.
Behind my sternum, password-locked,
a black-box file for every flight

that went down burning in the meeting
when they said *those people* and glanced
sideways, unaware the *those*
was sitting there in business casual,

nodding, taking careful notes.
I file the joke. I file the laugh.
I file the way my coffee cooled
while something in me learned to boil

so quietly it looked like calm.
I could recite each incident
with the flat voice of a flight recorder
found intact among the wreckage—

*and here you'll hear the moment where
the passenger stopped being human
in their eyes, and here, the silence
where I chose to keep my job.*

I am so *professional* it aches.
I am a knife wrapped up in cardigan.
I say *of course* and *happy to*
and *let's connect on that offline*—

and offline, in the file, I keep
the truer verb I never send,
red draft I write and don't hit *send* on,
the one that ends in nobody's *Best.*

They'll never know how gently held
their throats are in my level tone,
how mercy is the thing I practice
forty hours every week,

how the smile they trust to mean *no problem*
is a lid I set on something molten,
how I go home and the file grows heavier,
how I have never raised my voice,

how they mistake my grace for absence,
my silence for a kind of blessing—
when it's only me, still human, choosing,
one professional day at a time,

to let them live inside my kindness
they will never once deserve.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a long, autobiographical poem full of specific brand names and mundane details (Steak & Ale, AT&T, fondue in Zurich) that builds toward an unsettling meditation on suppression, resentment, and violence.
counterfactuals.output:
**Inventory**

I ate my birthdays at the Steak & Ale,
the salad bar a monument of chickpeas,
bacon bits like something scraped from teeth,
the wooden bowl, the ranch, the sneeze-guard glass
between my hunger and the world's provisions.
My father paid in twenties, tipped in silence.

We had AT&T. The phone was gold
and cradled in the kitchen like a relic.
Long distance was a sin we rarely sinned.
My mother's voice went thin across the wire
to Ohio, to her mother, dying slow,
the seconds ticking money we could hear.

In Zurich once, on someone else's card,
I ate the fondue at a place with flags,
the bread on little forks, the Kirsch, the burn,
the fat congealing on the copper pot.
I was in love. I thought that this was living.
The tram outside said *SBB* in white.

I owned a Trapper Keeper. Velcro sang
each time I opened it to nothing much.
I owned a Members Only jacket, tan,
the epaulets a promise no one kept.
I drank the Tab my mother wouldn't finish,
the aftertaste of pink, of pennies, of her.

Here is the thing they never tell you: how
the mundane is a lid you screw on tight.
The Tupperware of it. The airless seal.
You put the small humiliations in—
the coach who called you *sweetheart* as a slur,
the uncle's hand, the teacher's marking pen—

and burp the air out. Store them in the dark.
The refrigerator hum of decent people.
I learned to smile the way you fold a napkin.
I learned the Hallmark grammar of the card:
*Thinking of you. Get well. With Deepest Sympathy.*
The cursive gold. The dove. The nothing said.

You cannot keep it sealed forever, though.
The Tupperware remembers what it held.
The onion smell that stays in the plastic wall
no matter how you scrub it in the sink
with Dawn, with the yellow gloves, with your whole arm—
it stays. The container becomes the thing.

I want to tell you what I did not do.
I did not smash the sneeze-guard with my fist.
I did not rip the gold phone from the wall
and call my mother's mother back to life
and back to answer for the loveless house
she folded into my mother, who folded me.

I sat in Zurich eating melted cheese
and felt the thing rise up behind my sternum,
the years of it, the Members Only years,
the Trapper Keeper velcro of my rage
tearing and tearing at the smallest sound,
and I said, *This is lovely.* And I meant it.

That is the violence no one photographs:
the moment you agree to be the lid.
You clench the jaw that wants to open wide
and howl the Steak & Ale down to its studs.
You tip in silence. You say thank you. You
become the very quiet that was done to you.

And somewhere in the man who tips in silence
there is a boy still standing at the salad bar,
his wooden bowl held out, his knuckles white,
deciding, in the sneeze-guard's cloudy glass,
whether to fill it, or to lift it high,
or bring it down on someone. Anyone.

He fills it. Chickpeas. Bacon bits. The ranch.
He carries it back carefully to the table.
He does not spill. He has never spilled.
The AT&T of him keeps every line
connected, humming, billed by the cold second,
the charge accruing somewhere down the wire.

I pay. I always pay. In twenties. Smiling.
The fondue hardens. Someone says my name.
I turn. I am so pleasant it could kill.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
